She deposits [MATH: \[math]200] at the beginning of January, [MATH: \[/math]210] at the beginning of February, [MATH: \[math]220] at the beginning of March, and so on. If this trend continues, how much money will she have in the account at the end of July, assuming that the account earns no interest?

Content:
Giorgia's initial deposit was [MATH: \[/math]200,] and her monthly deposits increase by [MATH: \[math]10] per month. Therefore, the amount of money she deposits in month [MATH: n] can be modeled as an arithmetic sequence, as follows:

Content:
- The first term is [MATH: a_1=200.]
- The common difference is [MATH: d=10.]
- The total number of terms is [MATH: N=7] (since Giorgia made the last payment in July, the [MATH: 7]th month of the year).

Content:
To find the total amount of money in the account at the end of July, we have to calculate the sum of an arithmetic series. To do that, we use the formula
[MATH: S_N = \dfrac N 2 (2a_1 + (N-1)d).]

Content:
Substituting our values into the above, we get

Content:
[MATH: S_{7}|= (7)/(2)(2(200) + (7 − 1) ⋅ 10); = (7)/(2)(400 + 6 ⋅ 10); = (7)/(2)(460); = 1610.]
